one_liner: Ahead-of-time TypeScript-to-native compiler (SWC + LLVM); beats Node/V8 on some numeric and JSON micro-benchmarks, loses others.
what_it_does: Perry compiles a practical subset of TypeScript (plain JavaScript too) into a standalone native executable, with no JavaScript engine shipped; `perry compile src/main.ts -o app` replaces `node main.js`. It bundles native re-implementations of about 53 node:* modules and claims about 97% of Node's own tests pass, plus native UI and mobile/watch targets. It is not a JIT and not a library: you swap the runtime, not an API.
how_it_is_fast: SWC parses the TypeScript and Perry lowers it to LLVM IR (LLVM 22, in-process), so hot loops get ahead-of-time LLVM optimisation with no warm-up. Type inference narrows `number` to i64/i32 where a function only does integer work (fib uses integer add/compare, `i % 1000` becomes `srem` instead of an fmod call), proves `for (i < arr.length)` loops in-bounds and vectorises them, and a scalar-replacement pass removes short-lived object allocations. A generational GC and NaN-boxed values handle the dynamic remainder; fast-math (reassoc/contract) is opt-in via `--fast-math` since v0.5.585.
when_to_use: CLI tools and services written in TypeScript where startup time, a single small binary (from about 330 KB) and low RSS matter more than peak JIT throughput.
Integer- or f64-heavy recursive or loop code with stable types, e.g. recursive fib: 338 ms vs Node v22.23.1 912 ms in the project's 2026-09-23 correctness-checked artifact on Apple M1.
JSON parse/stringify round-trips and small JSON pipelines: json_roundtrip 144 ms vs Node 379-392 ms, 100-record pipeline 55.7 vs 100.0 ms in the same artifact.
Shipping TypeScript to targets Node cannot run on (iOS, Android, watchOS, tvOS) with native widgets.
when_not_to_use: Compute kernels over Buffer/Uint8Array: the project's own 2026-09-23 artifact (Perry 0.5.1639, Apple M1) has the 4K 5x5 image convolution at 2,266 ms vs Node 1,220 ms and Bun 888 ms, i.e. Perry 1.86x slower than Node (derived from page data), the opposite of the README headline.

Class-method-heavy or allocation-heavy object code: method_calls 35 vs 11 ms, binary_trees 13 vs 6 ms, object_create 8 vs 5 ms against Node in the same artifact; large JSON (500k records) 2,123 vs 864 ms.
Regex- or promise-heavy code: regex_replace 754 ms vs Node 98 ms and promise_all_chains 86 vs 59 ms in the artifact's app_patterns component.
Code that relies on runtime eval, runtime-computed dynamic import(), runtime-installed npm plugins or runtime type validation: these compile to deferred throws or are unsupported.

Teams that cannot absorb compiler bugs: the issue tracker shows recent silent miscompilations (#9278: stores to a module-global Buffer dropped, closed 2026-09-01; #9717 private-field array losing contents).

integration.form: Rust-built compiler CLI producing standalone executables (installed via npm @perryts/perry, Homebrew, winget, APT or Scoop)
integration.dependencies: Prebuilt binary: none at runtime. Building from source: pinned Rust nightly-2026-10-04, LLVM 22 development files, libclang (bindgen for libsqlite3-sys), system C compiler.
integration.min_toolchain: Rust nightly-2026-10-04 and LLVM 22 to build Perry itself; input is TypeScript (a supported subset)
integration.platforms: macOS, Linux, Windows, iOS, Android, watchOS, tvOS, visionOS natively; JavaScript or WebAssembly output for the web
integration.thread_safety: Real OS threads via parallelMap/spawn from perry/thread; closures are deep-copied across threads and the compiler rejects shared mutable state, except explicit shared memory used with Atomics.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: replaces `node app.js` with a compiled binary and re-implements most node:* modules, but no runtime-built eval/new Function, no runtime-computed dynamic import of uncompiled code, and type annotations are not enforced at runtime

gotchas: Harness finding: the README's lead row (image convolution 354 ms vs Node 1,207 ms, 3.4x) is pinned to v0.5.908 (2026-05-14). The workload source is byte-identical at HEAD, yet the project's own correctness-gated artifact benchmarks/results/public-node-bun-v1.json (Perry 0.5.1639, Node v22.23.1, Apple M1, 2026-09-23) measures Perry at 2,266 ms vs Node 1,220 ms, and HEAD REPORT.md (v0.5.1519, x86_64) has 1,204 vs 975 ms. That is a roughly 6x Perry regression on unchanged code, and the README still advertises the old figure, although benchmarks/README.md itself says the v0.5.908 tables are historical and the versioned artifact is authoritative where they differ. The cause is not documented; the x86 sweep is dated 2026-09-01, the day #9278 closed, and #9278 (a silent miscompilation that dropped stores to a module-global Buffer and gave this exact convolution workload a wrong checksum on 0.5.1220) hit the same code pattern.

The 6.2x 'accumulate' win (Perry 97 vs Node 597 ms on Node v25.8.0) does not hold on Node v22.23.1: the 2026-09-23 artifact has Perry 94 vs Node 95 ms. The gap depends on whether that V8 version inlines fmod for `i % 1000`, so it is not a Perry property. The Perry/Node 'accumulate' row is produced by suite/13_factorial.ts, whose header says it computes no factorial.

The polyglot table compares workloads that are not identical across languages. bench.cpp's nested_loops sums a 9M-element flat array while the TS version sums arr[i]+arr[j] over a 3,000-element array; fib is int in bench.cpp and i64 in bench.rs; math_intensive and object_create use different start values. RESULTS.md says all use f64 and identical algorithms. Only the Perry/Node/Bun columns run the same source, and only the public-JSON mode checks that their outputs agree (RESULTS_AUTO.md does not). Timing is in-process Date.now() at 1 ms resolution, so the 1-9 ms cells (array_write, object_create, array_read) sit at clock resolution.

RESULTS.md's loop_overhead prose describes an old `sum += 1.0` kernel that HEAD replaced with an Math.imul FNV recurrence because the old one folded to near zero. Its 12 ms --fast-math and 97 ms default figures therefore come from a different benchmark than the one in the suite now, and the current kernel ties Node (125 vs 126 ms on M1).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Perry over katsu or Graal.js when you want an existing TypeScript/Node codebase compiled AOT to one native binary, possibly for mobile or watch targets, and your hot paths are typed numeric loops or JSON. Stay on V8 (or pick Graal.js for peak JIT throughput) when the workload is method dispatch, regex, promises or byte-buffer kernels, where Perry's own data shows it losing.
verified_claims_summary: Project-run, same-source comparisons against Node (V8): on Apple M1 Max with Perry v0.5.908 and Node v25.8.0, recursive fib(40) took 309 vs 987 ms and the modulo loop 97 vs 597 ms, with three ties and a loss. The newer 2026-09-23 correctness-checked artifact (Perry 0.5.1639, Node v22.23.1, Bun 1.3.14, Apple M1) keeps the fib win (338 vs 912 ms) and the JSON round-trip win (144 vs 379-392 ms). In that artifact the modulo-loop gap closes to a tie (94 vs 95 ms), and Perry is slower than Node on image convolution (2,266 vs 1,220 ms), 500k-record JSON, method calls, binary trees, regex and promises.
status_note: Very active (last commit 2026-10-06, version 0.5.1657 in Cargo.toml, 4.9k stars), MIT. The project publishes raw samples and correctness-checked results, but its README headline numbers are older than, and in two rows contradicted by, its own newest artifact, and recent issues include silent miscompilations, so verify output and speed on your own workload before adopting.
